Dad's Preferences, Sourced and Dated

One page for what was noted, who heard it from him, and when.

Download PDF

How Dad likes his eggs is in your head, his Sunday routine is in your brother's, and the note from his doctor's office is somewhere in a kitchen drawer.

This page doesn't ask you to write any of it out again, or to work out what any of it means. It asks where each note is, who it came from, and its date.

What's been notedWhere the note isWho it came fromIts date
What he calls a good day
His morning routine
His evening routine
Meals he enjoys, and his usual times
Foods he'd rather not have, as a matter of taste
Allergies, if he has any, and where they're written down
Anything a doctor has told him about food or drink
The activities and people he looks forward to
How he likes to be addressed and spoken to
What helps him when he's somewhere unfamiliar
What he's said may be shared, and with whom

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will ask

Any row with an empty line, and any row where the note came from someone other than Dad. Put a name next to each. It doesn't need a date.

For example Evening routine: nobody has asked him. I'll bring it up at Sunday lunch. The fish: my sister says allergy, Dad says taste. Dad will mention it at his next regular visit.

How to use it

  • Under “Who it came from,” write “Dad” only if he said it himself. If it's something a relative remembers, write the relative's name.
  • Write the date of the conversation, or the date printed on the paper. If there isn't one, write “undated.”
  • Don't copy a doctor's note onto this page or put it in your own words. Just say where it is.
  • Keep the page where the family can find it, and change the date whenever Dad confirms something or changes it.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any record or instruction means, and it doesn't say whose version is right when two notes differ. A question about a written instruction goes to the person who wrote it. A question about what Dad likes goes to Dad.

Ready for the next step?

You know where each note about Dad's preferences is, who it came from and how recent it is. The care interview gives them one home: it goes through Dad's situation area by area, so the notes sit together with the rest of what you know, and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.
